reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / GeneReviews mitochondrial disease
clinicalPearls: The core triad is a sensory peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar ataxia and pigmentary retinopathy (retinitis pigmentosa), often with developmental delay and seizures
It is caused by maternally inherited mutations of the mitochondrial MT-ATP6 gene, most commonly m.8993T>G, which impair complex V (ATP synthase)
NARP and maternally inherited Leigh syndrome form a continuum: the same mutation produces NARP at intermediate mutant load and a Leigh phenotype when heteroplasmy is very high
The threshold effect means clinical severity tracks the proportion of mutant mitochondrial DNA in affected tissues
Retinal disease may present with night blindness and constricted visual fields, and salt-and-pepper or bone-spicule pigmentary changes are seen on fundoscopy
Lactate is often normal or only mildly elevated, unlike some other mitochondrial disorders, so a normal lactate does not exclude the diagnosis
Care is supportive, including neurorehabilitation, low-vision support, seizure management and avoidance of mitochondrial toxins
reference.pathophysiology: NARP arises from point mutations in MT-ATP6, which encodes a subunit of ATP synthase (respiratory-chain complex V). The mutations impair proton flux through the enzyme and reduce ATP generation while altering mitochondrial membrane potential. Because the gene is mitochondrial, inheritance is maternal and the mutation is heteroplasmic, so the phenotype depends on the mutant load within energy-dependent tissues. Neurons of the peripheral nerves, cerebellum and retina, which have high and sustained energy requirements, are preferentially affected, producing the neuropathy, ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa. At very high mutant proportions the same defect causes the more severe maternally inherited Leigh phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Maternally inherited Leigh syndrome (same gene, higher mutant load)
Other syndromic retinitis pigmentosa such as Bardet-Biedl or Usher syndrome
Kearns-Sayre syndrome and other mitochondrial retinopathies
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing for MT-ATP6 mutations (m.8993T>G / m.8993T>C) with heteroplasmy quantification
Ophthalmological assessment with fundoscopy and electroretinography
Nerve conduction studies to characterise the peripheral neuropathy
Brain MRI, which may show cerebellar atrophy or, at high mutant load, Leigh-type lesions
Resting and post-exercise lactate, recognising these are often normal
redFlags: Rapid clinical deterioration suggesting evolution towards a Leigh phenotype
Progressive visual loss impairing safety and function
reference.prognosis: NARP tends to run a slowly progressive course with episodic worsening during metabolic stress; visual, sensory and cerebellar disability accumulate over time, and prognosis is worse at high mutant loads where a Leigh-type picture may supervene.
pitfalls: Excluding a mitochondrial disorder because lactate is normal, which is common in NARP
Failing to recognise the NARP-Leigh continuum and its dependence on heteroplasmy level
Attributing retinitis pigmentosa to an isolated retinal dystrophy and missing the systemic mitochondrial cause
Not counselling about maternal inheritance and variable transmission of mutant load to offspring
references: GeneReviews: Mitochondrial DNA-Associated Leigh Syndrome and NARP
management: Provide symptomatic and supportive care as no curative therapy exists, treating seizures with anticonvulsants while avoiding mitochondrial-toxic agents such as valproate where possible
Offer low-vision support and ophthalmological management for retinitis pigmentosa, with neurorehabilitation and physiotherapy for ataxia and sensory neuropathy
Consider a mitochondrial cofactor regimen such as coenzyme Q10, riboflavin and other vitamins, recognising the limited supporting evidence
Avoid metabolic decompensation triggers such as prolonged fasting and mitochondrial-toxic drugs including aminoglycosides, and treat intercurrent illness promptly
Monitor for evolving multisystem involvement and progression towards a Leigh-type phenotype, with developmental assessment in children
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, ophthalmology, metabolic medicine and rehabilitation
Offer genetic counselling for maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance, explaining heteroplasmy and the threshold effect, with reproductive options including oocyte or mitochondrial donation
